title: Phone keypad words
label: idb
statement:
Given:

KNOWN_WORDS =
[
"careers",
"linkedin",
"hiring",
"interview",
"linkedgo"
]

Given a phone number, return all known words matching the phone keypad mapping.

Examples:

2273377 → ["careers"]

54653346 → ["linkedin", "linkedgo"]

flaw.ctx: You asked for words matching a phone number.
flaw.answer: `index / 3` assumes every key has three letters. It does not: 7 is **pqrs** and 9 is **wxyz**. So `s` lands on 8, `v` on 9, and `y` and `z` on `':'`, which is not a key at all — while `t`, `u`, `w` and `x` happen to come out right, which is why a quick spot-check passes. `careers` has an `s`, so 2273377 finds nothing.
flaw.fix: Use an explicit 26-entry table (or the eight key strings) rather than arithmetic.
flaw.verified: compiled against this problem's stage tests by npm run verify

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given:
> 
> KNOWN_WORDS =
> [
> "careers",
> "linkedin",
> "hiring",
> "interview",
> "linkedgo"
> ]
> 
> Given a phone number, return all known words matching the phone keypad mapping.
> 
> Examples:
> 
> 2273377 → ["careers"]
> 
> 54653346 → ["linkedin", "linkedgo"]

A keypad maps letters onto digits, many to one. Given a number, find which of a known set of words someone could have been typing.

Every word in the dictionary whose digit signature equals the input. A list, because the mapping is many-to-one — `linkedin` and `linkedgo` are indistinguishable on a keypad.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Letters only, case-insensitive, mapped a–z. | A word with an apostrophe or a hyphen has no keypad representation. I skip such words at build time rather than throwing, so one odd dictionary entry cannot break the service. |
| Digits 2–9 only; 0 and 1 carry no letters. | A number containing 0 or 1 can never match a word, so it returns empty. Worth saying, because it is a free early exit. |
| Exact-length match in the base problem. | The prefix version — which is what a phone actually does while you type — needs a trie, not a hash map. That is the follow-up. |
| The dictionary is large and the query rate is high. | The justification for O(N·L) preprocessing. If the dictionary changed on every query, the preprocessing would be waste and a scan would be better — state the ratio you are assuming. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
The reflex, especially if you have seen LeetCode 17, is to generate every letter string the number could spell and test each against the dictionary. `54653346` has 3×3×3×3×3×3×3×3 ≈ 6,500 candidates for eight digits, and a longer number is far worse. **That is the wrong direction**, and noticing that is the insight.

Go the other way. The letter → digit mapping is a **function**: every word has exactly one digit signature, and computing it is O(L). The number **is** a signature. So precompute the signature of every dictionary word, index the words by it, and a query becomes a single hash lookup.

Two things make this the right answer and both are worth saying. The direction with the many-to-one mapping is the cheap direction — you compute the canonical form rather than enumerating its preimages. And the work depends only on the **dictionary**, not on the query, so it happens once.

That is the same move as Q8’s wildcard index and the same as `244 Shortest Word Distance II`: *find a canonical key under which the expensive comparison becomes a hash lookup.* Three questions on this page use it, which is why it is worth naming as a pattern.

The hash map is exact-match only. A real phone shows candidates **while you type**, which is a prefix query, and a hash map cannot do prefixes at all. That is what the trie is for — and it is worth introducing it as the answer to a requirement rather than as the fancier structure.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Two options, both bad in different ways. **Generate**: enumerate every letter combination of the number and check each against the dictionary. **Scan**: for each query, compute every dictionary word’s signature and compare. *Generate is O(4^L) — up to 4 letters per digit. Scan is O(N · L) **per query**.*

**Why not good enough.** Generating is exponential and is the trap the LeetCode-17 instinct leads you into: it enumerates up to 65,000 strings for a nine-digit number to find at most a handful of real words. Scanning is merely wasteful, and the waste has a name — it recomputes per query something that is a property of the dictionary. Both are worth stating, because the *reason* each is wrong is different, and the second reason is the one that leads to the answer.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | A known word list at construction; a digit string per query |
| TRANSFORMATION | Each word → its digit signature, via a 26-entry lookup table |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `Dictionary<string, List<string>>` from signature to the words sharing it |
| ALGORITHM | Build once; a query is one hash lookup |
| OUTPUT | Every known word matching the number |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Build the 26-entry digit table from the eight keypad groups.
- For each known word, compute its signature; skip it if untypable.
- Append the word to `_bySignature[signature]`.
- Query: look up the number. Return a copy of the bucket, or an empty list.

- The dictionary is known **up front**, which is the constraint the whole design turns on.
- Word length equals number length in the base problem — an exact match, not a prefix.
- Many words collapse onto one signature, so the return type is plural.
- Queries are expected to outnumber dictionary changes by a wide margin. That ratio is the argument for preprocessing.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `Dictionary<string, List<string>>`, value a **list** | Because the mapping is many-to-one — the supplied example proves it. A `Dictionary<string, string>` would silently keep only the last word per signature and pass the first example. |
| A 26-entry `int[]` for letter → digit | Built once, statically. Array indexing beats a dictionary lookup or a chain of range comparisons, and it makes `Signature` a tight loop. |
| `StringComparer.Ordinal` | Signatures are digit strings, so culture-aware comparison is meaningless overhead — and in the general case it can treat distinct strings as equal, which would merge buckets. |
| `Signature` returns null for an untypable word | Rather than throwing. One word with an apostrophe should not fail the whole build. Skipping is the total, defensive choice. |
| A trie **only** for the prefix follow-up | The hash map is strictly better for exact match: O(L) versus O(L) but with no per-character node hop and far less memory. The trie earns its place when prefixes are required, and not before. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`BuildDigitTable` runs once, statically.** A `static readonly int[] DigitOf` initialised from the eight group strings. Writing the 26 entries by hand would be a transcription error waiting to happen; deriving them from `"abc"`, `"def"`, … makes the keypad layout the single source of truth and is self-documenting.

**Why the bucket value is a `List<string>`.** The supplied example requires it. A `Dictionary<string, string>` would pass the first example, fail the second, and the failure would look like a data problem rather than a design one.

**`Signature` returns null rather than throwing.** A dictionary of real words will eventually contain `o’brien` or `well-known`. Returning null and skipping means one unusual entry does not take the build down. The caller-visible behaviour is "that word can never be matched", which is exactly true.

**`new List<string>(hits)` on the way out.** Returning the internal list would let a caller mutate the index. One copy per query is cheap and the bucket is tiny; handing out internal state is the kind of thing that causes a bug six months later in an unrelated file.

**The trie is indexed by **digit**, not by letter.** `Node.Next` is a 10-element array indexed `0..9`, so walking the trie consumes the query directly with no translation. Indexing by letter would need the query converted to letters first, which is the exponential direction again — the structure choice quietly encodes the insight.

**`cur.Next[i] ??= new Node();`.** Null-coalescing assignment: create the child if absent, then use it. Three lines in one, and it is the idiomatic C# for trie insertion.

**`Words` is a list on the node, and is lazily allocated.** `(cur.Words ??= new List<string>()).Add(word)` — most trie nodes are internal and hold no words, so allocating a list per node would multiply the memory for nothing. On a large dictionary that is the difference between a trie that fits and one that does not.

**`WithPrefix` collects the whole subtree.** `Collect` walks every descendant. That is O(matches + nodes below), which is the honest cost: a one-digit prefix on a large dictionary returns almost everything. A real autocomplete caps the result count, and the cap has to be applied **during** the walk to be worth anything.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| build | O(N · L) | O(N · L) | One signature per word, each O(L) |
| `WordsFor` (exact) | O(L + m) | O(m) | One hash of an L-digit string, plus copying m matches |
| `Signature` | O(L) | O(L) | One table lookup per character |
| trie `Add` | O(L) | O(L) nodes worst case | One node per digit, shared with existing words |
| trie `Exact` | O(L) | O(m) | L node hops |
| trie `WithPrefix` | O(L + nodes in the subtree) | O(m) | The subtree walk is the cost |

**The hash map and the trie are both O(L) for exact match, and the hash map is still the right choice.** One hash computation beats L pointer dereferences for cache reasons, and the trie costs far more memory. The trie wins exactly one thing — prefix queries — and that is the entire argument for it. Reaching for the trie on the exact-match problem because it is the more sophisticated structure is the mistake this question is set up to catch.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Empty number | Returns empty, checked first. |
| Number containing 0 or 1 | No word can match; returns empty. A free early exit. |
| Number shorter than every word | Empty in the base problem — a prefix is not a match. |
| No matching word | Empty list, not null. A caller should never have to null-check a collection return. |
| Several words, one signature | All returned. The supplied second example. |
| Untypable word in the dictionary | Skipped at build time, never matched. |
| Mixed-case dictionary | Lower-cased in `Signature`, so `LinkedIn` and `linkedin` share a signature. |
| Duplicate word in the dictionary | Appears twice in its bucket. De-duplicate at build time if that is wrong — state the choice. |
| Very large dictionary | Build is O(N·L) and memory is the signature strings plus the word references. The trie would be considerably larger. |

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md: **Verification exercise:** Incorrect mapping — `index / 3` assumes every key has three letters. It does not: 7 is **pqrs** and 9 is **wxyz**. So `s` lands on 8, `v` on 9, and `y` and `z` on `':'`, which is not a key at all — while `t`, `u`, `w` and `x` happen to come out right, which is why a quick spot-check passes. `careers` has an `s`, so 2273377 finds nothing.

learn.md:
**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Words are added while lookups run.* — Copy-on-write the dictionary, or a reader/writer lock — reads dominate

- *Suggest as the user types.* — A trie on digit signatures

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Return matches while the user is still typing.**

A trie keyed on digits. Each node is a digit; words hang off the node where they end. Walk the prefix in O(L), then collect the subtree. In production, cap the results during the walk and order the node’s words by frequency so the cap keeps the best ones.

*Trade-off:* Prefix capability for memory and cache locality. The trie is much larger than the hash map and each step is a pointer chase. It is also the structure that makes "show me something useful after three digits" possible at all, so when the requirement is there it is not really a trade.

**The dictionary is 500,000 words and must be memory-efficient.**

For the hash map, the waste is the signature **strings**: one allocation per distinct signature. For words up to 9 digits a signature fits in a `long` (9 digits × 4 bits, or just base-8 since digits are 2–9), so the key becomes a value type and the string allocations disappear along with their hashing cost. For the trie, the fix is a compressed form — a radix tree merging single-child chains, or a double-array trie — which cuts node count substantially.

*Trade-off:* The `long` key is a large, cheap win and caps word length at 9 digits, which has to be checked rather than assumed. A radix tree is a real reduction and much more code. I would do the `long` key first and measure before touching the trie.

**The dictionary changes at runtime.**

Adding a word is one signature and one list append, O(L). Removing needs the word pulled from its bucket, which is a linear scan of that bucket — fine, since buckets are tiny, but worth naming. In the trie, removal means unlinking from the terminal node and optionally pruning now-empty nodes upward.

*Trade-off:* For a mostly-static dictionary with occasional additions, do nothing clever. If updates were frequent I would rebuild into a new index and swap the reference atomically, so readers never see a half-built structure — which is cheaper to reason about than making the index itself thread-safe.

**Also match words that are longer than the number, or allow one typo.**

One typo means "signatures within edit distance 1", which cannot be hashed for directly. The wildcard-index trick from Q8 applies: index each signature under every single-digit blanking, so `2273377` also goes under `*273377`, `2*73377` and so on. A query then does L lookups. For general edit distance, the trie plus a bounded DFS with an edit budget is the standard answer.

*Trade-off:* The wildcard index multiplies memory by L and handles exactly one substitution. The trie walk with a budget handles any distance and costs a search rather than a lookup. Both are big steps up from exact match, so I would want to know how many typos actually need handling before choosing — "one substitution" and "any edit" are very different bills.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Digits 0 and 1? Upper-case words? Empty number?* — No letters on 0/1 → no match; normalise case; empty → none

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Lookup cost?* — O(L) after O(total letters) preprocessing
